title: Behavioral Patterns: Who Does What, and When
oneLiner: Strategy, Observer, Command, State, Template Method, Iterator and Chain of Responsibility, with C# and the .NET features built on them.
keyTakeaway: Behavioral patterns decide how responsibility and control flow are split between objects. Most of them replace a growing if/else or switch with objects: one object per algorithm (Strategy), per state (State), per request (Command) or per handler (Chain of Responsibility). If you can say which question a branch is answering, you can usually say which pattern replaces it.
explanation:
These patterns are the ones you use every day in .NET without naming them. `foreach` runs on the Iterator pattern. Every C# `event` is Observer. ASP.NET Core middleware is Chain of Responsibility. `BackgroundService` is Template Method. Recognizing them in the framework is the fastest way to remember them, and it gives you concrete answers when an interviewer asks "where have you used this?"

Two pairs here are the most confused in the whole catalog. Strategy and State have the same class diagram; the difference is who picks the implementation (the caller, or the object itself as it moves between states). Strategy and Template Method solve the same problem, varying one part of an algorithm, with composition versus inheritance.

Pick a pattern. Each one shows the intent, when to use it and when not to, a small structure diagram, idiomatic C#, where it already lives in .NET or this app, and the interview angle.
